assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measuring resource misallocation across firms and linking it to cross-country TFP and income differences gave growth and development economics a quantitative framework that is now standard. It has shaped how researchers and policy institutions analyse productivity gaps.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the central measurement and quantification contribution. Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is a closely parallel contribution and Restuccia is credited on the ballot. The three-name cap forces a hard choice, and I propose the two most associated with the canonical measurement framework.
assessment.maturity: The core work is about 15 to 18 years old and has been extensively replicated, extended and applied, so impact is well established.
uncertainties: Priority between Restuccia and Rogerson and Hsieh and Klenow could be argued either way.
Measured misallocation is sensitive to measurement error and to markup and distortion assumptions.
I am relying on my own knowledge of the literature, with no independent verification.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The trade-shock and labour-market adjustment research changed how economists and policymakers understand the distributional costs of trade and technology. It shows persistent local labour-market effects and has reshaped debates in trade, labour and political economy.
assessment.attribution: Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the joint authors of the China shock papers and are the natural trio. Katz is credited on the ballot for the earlier task and skill-bias literature, but the cap and the specificity of the China shock work favour these three.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from around 2013 to 2016 and has been heavily replicated and debated, including on its long-run magnitudes. It is mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: Debate persists over long-run magnitudes and identification.
The task-based framework involves other scholars not listed.
The ballot item merges two related literatures, so the prize motivation could be framed in different ways.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built modern political economics by analysing how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal and economic outcomes. It is both a theoretical and an empirical research programme that has opened up a large field.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core pair through their joint books and papers on political economics. Besley and Persson are closely linked through the state-capacity work, and Besley is credited on the ballot. A trio is defensible, though the weight of each contribution varies by strand.
assessment.maturity: The work spans more than 25 years and is very well confirmed, with a large downstream literature. It has long been regarded as a prize-calibre area.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would reward the field as a whole or a narrower strand.
Credit allocation within the trio is uncertain.
Part of the empirical evidence on constitutional effects is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin modern monetary policy analysis and central-bank modelling. This is among the most consequential macroeconomic frameworks of recent decades.
assessment.attribution: Credit is highly dispersed across eight names. Calvo's pricing model, Woodford's monetary theory and Gali's New Keynesian synthesis and empirical work are central, but Taylor, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets are also very important. A three-name cap makes any selection contestable.
assessment.maturity: The work is decades old and has been validated by practice, though its empirical record was tested by the financial crisis and the post-pandemic inflation.
uncertainties: Attribution is highly diffuse and the three-name limit makes any selection contestable.
Empirical fit of the standard model was challenged by the financial crisis and post-pandemic inflation.
Overlap with other macro candidates such as heterogeneous-agent models.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed international trade theory and empirics by explaining exporter premia and gains from trade through reallocation across firms. It shaped a generation of quantitative trade research.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution, and Helpman's earlier and related work on firm-level trade models is substantial. Redding is also credited on the ballot for quantitative extensions. I treat Melitz and Helpman as the core.
assessment.maturity: The framework is more than 20 years old and broadly confirmed, though quantitative gains-from-trade results depend on parametrisation.
uncertainties: Overlap with Helpman and Grossman (B046) and with the quantitative trade candidates.
Krugman's earlier prize partly covers the trade-theory space.
Credit allocation relative to Redding and others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Monopsony and imperfect competition in labour markets reframed how economists think about wage-setting, minimum wages and labour-market power. Empirical evidence now supports a view in which employers have wage-setting power.
assessment.attribution: Manning's work on monopsony in motion is the central synthesis. Ashenfelter contributed methods and early empirical work on wage-setting and labour-market evidence, and Naidu is credited for more recent work. I propose the first two as the more established contributors.
assessment.maturity: The area is established but the evidence continues to evolve. It is also partly recognised by the 2021 prize, which touched on minimum-wage and labour-market natural experiments.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2021 prize for Card and related work.
Magnitudes of monopsony power are debated.
Naidu's more recent contributions may be underweighted.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The reconstruction of long-run top-income series and wealth distributions changed the empirical foundation of inequality research and public debate. Its influence on both research and policy is very large.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez are the central pair for top-income series. Zucman has contributed on wealth and offshore wealth, but his contribution is more recent and partly derivative of the shared data programme.
assessment.maturity: The core data work is from the 2000s and has been widely adopted. Debates continue over measurement and interpretation, including capital-income dynamics and the policy conclusions.
uncertainties: Methodological criticism of the wealth and capital-share conclusions.
Possible concern about the policy advocacy surrounding parts of the work.
Saez is also credited in B003, so credit might be split across candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Mian and Sufi showed with granular data that household leverage and credit supply expansions drive booms and busts, and they linked household balance sheets to aggregate demand and the Great Recession. This is a substantive empirical and conceptual contribution to macro-finance.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the clear joint authors of the core research programme. Campbell is credited on the ballot for related household finance work, but his contribution is on a different axis.
assessment.maturity: The work is about 10 to 15 years old and has been confirmed in multiple settings, but it is more recent than most higher-ranked candidates.
uncertainties: Relative to older candidates the work is young and its long-run influence is still being assessed.
Some evidence on the credit supply interpretation is debated.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on banking and financial crises.
